question: What are the four pillars of object-oriented programming? Explain each briefly.
hint: Name encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism with a one-line example each.

points.text: Encapsulation: keeping data and the methods that use it together and hiding internal state
Abstraction: exposing only what is needed and hiding complexity
Inheritance: a class reusing and extending another class
Polymorphism: one interface, many forms (overloading and overriding)

question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
hint: Contrast compile-time and runtime polymorphism and mention the signature rules.

points.text: Overloading: same method name with different parameter lists in the same class
Overloading is resolved at compile time (static polymorphism)
Overriding: a subclass redefines a method of its parent with the same signature
Overriding is resolved at runtime (dynamic dispatch)

question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
hint: Talk about state, constructors, multiple inheritance and when you would choose each.

points.text: An abstract class can have fields (state), constructors and implemented methods
An interface defines a contract that classes implement
A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class
Choose an abstract class to share code in an is-a hierarchy, an interface for a capability

question: Explain the difference between an array and a linked list. When would you use each?
hint: Compare memory layout, access time and insertion cost.

points.text: Arrays store elements contiguously and allow O(1) access by index
Linked lists store nodes connected by pointers or references
Inserting or deleting in the middle is O(1) in a linked list (given the node) but O(n) in an array
Use arrays for frequent reads and cache-friendly loops; linked lists for frequent inserts and deletes

question: How does a hash map work internally?
hint: Explain hashing to buckets, collision handling, load factor and complexity.

points.text: A hash function maps each key to a bucket index
Collisions are handled by chaining (lists or trees) or open addressing
When the load factor is exceeded the table is resized and keys are rehashed
Average O(1) insert and lookup, O(n) in the worst case

question: Compare quicksort and merge sort. When would you prefer one over the other?
hint: Mention average and worst-case complexity, stability and memory.

points.text: Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case (bad pivots)
Merge sort is always O(n log n) and is stable
Merge sort needs O(n) extra memory; quicksort sorts in place
Prefer merge sort for linked lists, external sorting or when stability matters; quicksort for arrays in memory

question: How would you detect a cycle in a linked list?
hint: Floyd's fast and slow pointers, and the cost of the hash-set approach.

points.text: Use two pointers: a slow one moving one step and a fast one moving two steps (Floyd's algorithm)
If there is a cycle the pointers eventually meet; if fast reaches null there is none
It runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space
Alternative: store visited nodes in a hash set, which needs O(n) space

question: Explain BFS and DFS. Where would you use each?
hint: Data structures used, traversal order and typical applications.

points.text: BFS explores level by level using a queue
DFS goes deep first using a stack or recursion
BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph
DFS suits cycle detection, topological sort, connected components and mazes

question: What is dynamic programming? Explain it with an example problem.
hint: Overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, memoization vs tabulation, and a classic example.

points.text: The problem has overlapping subproblems that would be solved repeatedly
It has optimal substructure: the best answer is built from best answers of subproblems
Results are stored by memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up)
A concrete example such as Fibonacci, knapsack, coin change or longest common subsequence

question: What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF.
hint: Why we normalise, and the rule each normal form adds.

points.text: Normalization reduces redundancy and update, insert and delete anomalies
1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF: no partial dependency on part of a composite key
3NF: no transitive dependency between non-key attributes

question: What are the ACID properties of a database transaction?
hint: Define atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability with an example such as a bank transfer.

points.text: Atomicity: all or nothing
Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere
Durability: committed data survives crashes

question: What is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN?
hint: Which rows each returns, and what appears when there is no match.

points.text: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables
LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table
Unmatched right-side columns are NULL
A concrete example, e.g. employees and departments

question: What is a database index and what are its trade-offs?
hint: How it speeds up reads, how it is stored, and what it costs.

points.text: An index makes lookups and filtering faster
It is usually a B-tree (or hash) structure over the column values
It slows down inserts and updates and uses extra storage
Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY with good selectivity

question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
hint: Memory, cost of switching and communication.

points.text: A process has its own address space
Threads of a process share its memory
Thread switches are cheaper than process switches
Processes communicate through IPC; threads need synchronisation

question: What is a deadlock and how can it be prevented?
hint: Definition, the four Coffman conditions and prevention or avoidance.

points.text: Processes wait forever for resources held by each other
Four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
Prevention: break a condition, e.g. lock ordering or timeouts
Avoidance (Banker's algorithm) or detection and recovery

question: What is virtual memory and how does paging work?
hint: Pages, frames, page tables, TLB and page faults.

points.text: Virtual memory gives each process its own large address space
Memory is divided into fixed-size pages and frames
Page tables (cached in the TLB) translate virtual to physical addresses
A page fault loads a missing page from disk

question: What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
hint: DNS, TCP and TLS, the HTTP request and rendering.

points.text: DNS resolves the domain name to an IP address
A TCP connection (and TLS handshake for HTTPS) is set up
The browser sends an HTTP request and the server returns a response
The browser parses HTML, CSS and JavaScript and renders the page

question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
hint: Reliability, ordering, speed and typical uses.

points.text: TCP is connection-oriented, reliable and ordered
UDP is connectionless and faster but gives no delivery guarantee
Typical uses: TCP for web and email, UDP for streaming, gaming, DNS and calls
TCP has more overhead (handshake, larger header)

question: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
hint: Reference versus content comparison, with a String example.

points.text: == compares references (whether both point to the same object)
.equals() compares content or logical equality
Classes override equals() (and hashCode()) to define equality
Strings: two equal strings may be different objects (string pool)

question: Explain how garbage collection works in Java.
hint: Reachability, generations, collectors and memory leaks.

points.text: The JVM automatically frees objects that are no longer reachable
The heap is split into young and old generations
Collectors such as G1 mark live objects and sweep or compact the rest
Leaks still happen when references are kept unintentionally

question: What are checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
hint: Compile-time checking, examples and when to use each.

points.text: Checked exceptions are verified at compile time and must be caught or declared
Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and are not enforced
Checked for recoverable conditions, unchecked for programming errors
finally / try-with-resources to release resources

question: Is HashMap thread-safe? What would you use in a multi-threaded program?
hint: Race conditions, ConcurrentHashMap and trade-offs.

points.text: HashMap is not thread-safe; concurrent writes can corrupt it
ConcurrentHashMap allows safe concurrent access with fine-grained locking/CAS
Collections.synchronizedMap or explicit locks are alternatives
Trade-off between safety, contention and throughput

question: What is dependency injection and how does Spring implement it?
hint: Inversion of control, beans, the container and constructor injection.

points.text: Dependencies are provided from outside instead of created inside the class (inversion of control)
The Spring container creates and manages beans
Annotations such as @Component, @Service and constructor injection / @Autowired
It makes code easier to test (mocks) and change

question: How would you design a REST API for a library management system?
hint: Resources and URLs, HTTP methods, status codes and cross-cutting concerns.

points.text: Model resources as nouns such as /books, /members and /loans
Use HTTP methods for actions: GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, DELETE
Return proper status codes (200, 201, 400, 404)
Add validation, pagination, authentication and versioning

question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?
hint: Mutability, syntax, performance and use cases.

points.text: Lists are mutable; tuples are immutable
Lists use square brackets, tuples use parentheses
Tuples are hashable (usable as dictionary keys) and slightly faster
Tuples suit fixed records; lists suit collections that change

question: What are decorators in Python and where would you use them?
hint: Functions that wrap functions, the @ syntax and practical uses.

points.text: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a wrapped version
Applied with the @decorator syntax
Common uses: logging, timing, authentication, caching
They rely on closures; functools.wraps keeps metadata

question: What is the difference between var, let and const in JavaScript?
hint: Scope, hoisting and reassignment.

points.text: var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped
Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
const cannot be reassigned (objects can still be mutated)
Prefer const, then let; avoid var

question: What is the virtual DOM in React and why is it useful?
hint: In-memory tree, diffing (reconciliation) and minimal DOM updates.

points.text: A lightweight in-memory representation of the UI
React diffs the new and old trees (reconciliation)
Only the minimal changes are applied to the real DOM, in batches
Keys help React identify list items

question: What is overfitting and how can you prevent it?
hint: Definition, how to detect it, and regularisation techniques.

points.text: The model learns noise in the training data and generalises poorly
Detected by a gap between training and validation performance
Prevented with regularisation, dropout, more data, early stopping, cross-validation or simpler models
Related to the bias-variance trade-off

question: Explain precision, recall and F1-score. When would you prefer one over another?
hint: Formulas in words and an imbalanced-data example.

points.text: Precision: of the predicted positives, how many are correct
Recall: of the actual positives, how many were found
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall
Choose by the cost of errors, e.g. recall for disease screening, precision for spam

question: What is Docker, and how is a container different from a virtual machine?
hint: Images, the shared kernel and resource usage.

points.text: Docker packages an application with its dependencies into an image
Containers share the host operating system kernel
VMs run a full guest OS on a hypervisor
Containers start faster and use fewer resources

question: What is CI/CD and why do teams use it?
hint: Continuous integration, continuous delivery and tooling.

points.text: Continuous integration: every change is built and tested automatically
Continuous delivery/deployment: changes are released automatically or with one click
Tools such as GitHub Actions, Jenkins or GitLab CI run the pipeline
Benefits: fast feedback, fewer bugs and smaller, safer releases

question: Explain the difference between stack and heap memory.
hint: What lives where, allocation and lifetime.

points.text: The stack holds local variables and function call frames
The heap is for dynamic allocation (malloc/new)
The stack is small and fast; the heap is larger and can fragment
Stack memory is freed automatically; heap memory must be freed or collected

question: What does the volatile keyword mean in C and where is it used?
hint: Compiler optimisation, hardware registers and interrupts.

points.text: It tells the compiler not to optimise away or cache reads and writes
Used when the value can change outside the program's control
Examples: memory-mapped peripheral registers, flags set in interrupts
volatile does not make operations atomic or thread-safe

question: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
hint: How the attack works, an example and the right defences.

points.text: Untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL query and changes its meaning
Example: entering ' OR 1=1 -- to bypass a login
Use prepared statements or parameterised queries (or an ORM)
Also validate input and use least-privilege database accounts

question: How would you measure the success of a new feature in an app?
hint: Metrics, an A/B test, significance and guardrails.

points.text: Define the goal and the metric (conversion, retention, engagement)
Run an A/B test with a control group
Check statistical significance and sample size
Watch guardrail metrics such as revenue, latency or churn

question: Tell me about yourself.
hint: Two minutes: education, key skills and projects, one achievement, and why this role.

points.text: Your current education (degree, branch, college)
Your main skills and one or two projects
An achievement or experience that sets you apart
Why you are interested in this role

question: Why do you want to join our company?
hint: Show research about the company and connect it to your skills and goals.

points.text: Something specific you know about the company (product, mission, customers)
How your skills fit the role
What you want to learn and how you want to grow
A clear, specific reason rather than a generic answer

question: Describe a time you had a conflict in a team. How did you resolve it?
hint: Use STAR: situation, task, action, result.

points.text: Situation: the team, the project and the disagreement
Action: how you listened, discussed and found a compromise
Result: the outcome for the team or project
What you learned

question: Tell me about a project you are proud of. What was your role and what did you learn?
hint: Problem, your own contribution, technical decisions and measurable results.

points.text: The problem the project solves and who uses it
Your own role and contribution
Technologies and why you chose them
Results or impact (numbers if possible)

question: What is your biggest weakness?
hint: A real weakness, what you are doing about it and the progress so far.

points.text: A genuine weakness, stated honestly
Concrete steps you are taking to improve
Evidence of progress

question: Where do you see yourself in five years?
hint: Realistic growth that fits the company.

points.text: Growth in responsibility (e.g. senior engineer, leading a module)
Skills you want to master
Doing it in this company / contributing to its goals

question: Describe a situation where you had to meet a tight deadline.
hint: STAR with the way you prioritised.

points.text: The situation and the deadline
How you planned and prioritised
What you did
The result

question: Tell me about a time you failed. What did you learn?
hint: Own the mistake, show the lesson and what changed.

points.text: A concrete failure
Taking ownership
The lesson learned
What you do differently now

question: Why should we hire you?
hint: Match your skills to the role with evidence, then add attitude.

points.text: Skills that match the role
Evidence: projects, results or achievements
Attitude: learning, teamwork, ownership
The value you will add to the company

question: Tell me about a time you took the lead on something.
hint: STAR: what you led, how you motivated others, and the result.

points.text: The situation and why leadership was needed
What you did as the leader (planning, delegating, motivating)
The result
What you learned about leading people
